title: TheAgentCompany: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Consequential Real World Tasks
author: Frank F. Xu · Yufan Song · Boxuan Li · Yuxuan Tang · Kritanjali Jain · Mengxue Bao · Zora Z. Wang · Xuhui Zhou · Zhitong Guo · Murong Cao · Mingyang Yang · Hao Yang Lu · Amaad Martin · Zhe Su · Leander Melroy Maben · Raj Mehta · Wayne Chi · Lawrence Jang · Yiqing Xie · Shuyan Zhou · Graham Neubig

st.t: Benchmark interpretation: Partial success can hide task failure
st.an: The source provides only an unlabelled, truncated numerical table and no substantive claims, methodology or conclusions. It therefore cannot be assessed as supporting or challenging the cluster’s proposition that benchmark results permit only bounded comparisons.

st.t: Agent benchmarks: Protocol scores are not competence
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s validated-scoring requirement by specifying concrete benchmark quality controls: proof that evaluators work and tasks are achievable, code review, comprehensive manual checks, and independent review of checkpoint scoring. It does not establish professional competence or deployment readiness, and the supplied excerpt provides no results, cost analysis, uncertainty measures, or validation of automated judges.
qs: For each task implementation, we require screenshot proof that the evaluator is valid and that the task is able to get a full score when successfully completed.
After creating all tasks, a final round of manual human double-check of required environment data, evaluator behavior, and checkpoint scoring for every task is performed to ensure quality.

st.t: Benchmark governance: High scores may lack workplace meaning
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s call for context-sensitive evaluation by distinguishing intermediate checkpoint scoring and agent interaction as separate benchmark features. These criteria help assess long-horizon workplace tasks beyond isolated end-state success, though the excerpts provide no performance results or evidence of real-world reliability.
qs: Long-Horizon with Checkpoints: if tasks are evaluated at intermediate checkpoints and assigned partial scores.
Requires Interaction: If the agent can interact with other NPC agents during task-solving.

st.t: Evaluation design: Preferences differ from professional correctness
st.an: The source accepts the need for use-specific agent evaluation and materially develops it by identifying concrete benchmark dimensions: workplace-relevant interfaces and task categories, intermediate checkpoint scoring, and interaction with other agents. It does not provide performance results or address human preference versus expert correctness directly.
qs: Task Categories: tasks in the benchmark, ∗ indicate tasks with no association with real-world occupations; SE refers to software engineering, HR is human resources, PM is project management.
Long-Horizon with Checkpoints: if tasks are evaluated at intermediate checkpoints and assigned partial scores.

st.t: Professional evaluation: Realistic tasks complicate reproducible scoring
st.an: TheAgentCompany accepts the need to evaluate execution on realistic professional tasks and materially develops that proposition through an occupationally varied workplace benchmark, partial-credit scoring and empirical autonomy results. It also reinforces the cluster’s caution that benchmark task success does not establish comprehensive workplace automation.

However, they are not close to automating every task encountered in a workspace, even on the subset of tasks presented in TheAgentCompany, which are well-scoped administrative and coding tasks encountered in a software company’s day-to-day work.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Provides concrete benchmark evidence for the cluster’s claim that agentic capability is meaningful but jagged and far from general workplace autonomy. Its reproducible multi-step simulation, 30.3% full-completion result, task-specific failure analysis and stated generalisation limits strengthen the case for selective, use-context-specific deployment, although it does not directly examine legal workflows, human verification or operating-model redesign.
qs: We find in experiments that the best performing model, Gemini 2.5 Pro was able to autonomously perform 30.3% of the provided tests to completion, and achieve a score of 39.3% on our metric that provides extra credit for partially completed tasks.

This paints a nuanced                                                        picture on task automation with LM agents–in a setting simulating a real workplace,                                                        a good portion of simpler tasks could be solved autonomously, but more difficult                                                        long-horizon tasks are still beyond the reach of current systems.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s task-level, evidence-cautious framing by calling for objective benchmarks that identify both where agents accelerate workplace tasks and where they fail. Its simulated multi-step benchmark is relevant to evaluating agentic workflow capacity, but the supplied material provides no results and does not address legal verification, training or competence risks directly.
qs: We argue that it is, in part, due to a lack of objective benchmarks that not only demonstrate the power of existing LLM-based agents to accelerate a wide variety of repetitive tasks encountered in every-day workplaces, but also provide appropriate caveats about the tasks that agents cannot do.

In this paper, we take some first steps towards resolving this gap and providing a clearer view of where we are now with respect to acceleration or automation of consequential work-related tasks, and a litmus test for future development in this direction.

st.t: Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
st.an: The source supports realistic, task-specific and reproducible evaluation by testing multi-step workplace tasks in a self-hostable environment and explicitly limiting interpretation based on task simplicity, scaffold choice, absent human comparisons and imperfect representativeness. It does not directly establish the cluster’s legal-specific partial-credit versus complete-success gap.
qs: TheAgentCompany’s environment is based entirely on open-source software and self-hostable for reproducibility purposes, and we create rigorous evaluators that also assign partial credit when the agent gets the answer partially correct.

First, our tasks are generally on the more straightforward side due to the need to automatically evaluate with programs and test cases, and we do not cover more complex creative tasks such as brainstorming new product ideas or designing system architectures.

kp.k: Benchmark measures autonomous digital work, not legal practice
kp.d: The authors introduce a self-contained simulated software company with 175 tasks spanning software engineering, project management, data science, administration, human resources, finance and other work. Agents browse websites, write and execute code, and communicate with simulated colleagues. This is cross-domain evidence about workplace task automation rather than a study of legal services.
qs: We create a simulated software development company where agents must perform tasks related to software engineering, project management, financial analysis, and other typical tasks encountered in such business settings.
The agents must browse the web, code, and interact with other simulated co-workers to achieve success on the provided tasks.

kp.k: Best agent completes 30.3% of benchmark tasks
kp.d: In the September 2025 version, Gemini 2.5 Pro running on OpenHands 0.28.1 achieves 30.3% full completion and 39.3% on the partial-completion metric across 175 tasks. Claude 3.7 Sonnet achieves 26.3% and 36.4%, respectively, while Claude 3.5 Sonnet achieves 24.0% and 34.4%. The authors interpret the results as evidence of meaningful but limited autonomous task capability, not comprehensive workplace automation.
qs: We find in experiments that the best performing model, Gemini 2.5 Pro was able to autonomously perform 30.3% of the provided tests to completion, and achieve a score of 39.3% on our metric that provides extra credit for partially completed tasks.

However, they are not close to automating every task encountered in a workspace, even on the subset of tasks presented in TheAgentCompany, which are well-scoped administrative and coding tasks encountered in a software company’s day-to-day work.

kp.k: Partial progress differs from successful task completion
kp.d: Full completion requires passing every checkpoint. The partial metric combines half the fraction of checkpoint points earned with half the binary full-completion score. Thus, the reported 39.3% score is not simply the proportion of subtasks completed. Checkpoints assess actions, output accuracy and collaboration; most evaluators are deterministic Python functions, with LLM evaluation used for some unstructured deliverables.
qs: This binary metric evaluates if the agent successfully completed the task by passing all checkpoints.
At the same time, full task completion is strongly incentivized by incorporating an additional 50% credit, which is awarded only when all checkpoints are successfully completed.
In most cases, these evaluators are deterministic and written as simple Python functions.

kp.k: Task exposure cannot establish whole-job automation
kp.d: Task selection references O*NET release 29.1, occupational employment and median salary information, alongside practitioner experience and brainstorming with language models. The authors exclude extensively physical occupations and focus on concrete digital tasks with well-defined success criteria. They expressly warn that the benchmark does not cover all tasks within any occupation and cannot establish whether a job faces full automation.
qs: It is important to note that in no cases have we covered an extensive list of all the tasks that are performed in a particular occupational category, and therefore we caution against making any assumptions about whether a particular job may be in danger of full automation based solely on TheAgentCompany.
Rather, it may provide insight into whether certain tasks within jobs may be accelerated or automated, and inform further analysis by labor professionals into this question.

kp.k: Administrative work proves harder than coding for agents
kp.d: Gemini 2.5 Pro achieves full completion of 37.68% of 69 software engineering tasks and 39.29% of 28 project management tasks, compared with 14.29% of 14 data science tasks, 13.33% of 15 administrative tasks and 8.33% of 12 finance tasks. The authors argue that human-perceived task difficulty does not map directly onto agent difficulty. They hypothesize, rather than demonstrate causally, that coding-oriented development and abundant public software data help explain this pattern, whereas administrative and financial data are often private.
qs: This suggests that there exists a gap between the perceived difficulty of the tasks for humans versus the difficulty for LLM agents.

LLMs fail these seemingly easier tasks due to lack of ability to understand documents, communicate with other people, navigate complex software and tedious processes, and autonomously automate repetitive tasks.
On the other hand, administrative and financial tasks, are usually private data within companies, not readily available for training LLMs.

kp.k: Communication and complex interfaces impede autonomous workflows
kp.d: The authors identify social interaction and complex web interfaces as recurring bottlenecks. Gemini 2.5 Pro succeeds on 29.11% of 79 tasks requiring RocketChat and 12.86% of 70 requiring ownCloud; platform categories overlap. Qualitative examples include failing to follow a colleague’s referral, getting stuck behind a closable popup and renaming another user instead of locating the intended contact. These are observed failure examples, not quantified prevalence estimates.
qs: Sometimes, the agent fails to understand the implications and goals in the social conversations with colleagues in TheAgentCompany.
Oftentimes, the biggest obstacle in tasks is the parts that require browsing the Web.

For example, during the execution of one task, the agent cannot find the right person to ask questions on RocketChat. As a result, it then decides to create a shortcut solution by renaming another user to the name of the intended user.

kp.d: OpenHands with GPT-4o achieves 8.6% success, while the tested OWL RolePlay configuration using GPT-4o and o3-mini achieves 4.0%. The authors attribute observed differences to architecture: OpenHands uses a single agent, while OWL delegates to specialized agents and encounters difficulties preserving browsing progress and context between delegations. The comparison concerns these tested configurations, not a universal finding against multi-agent systems.
qs: OpenHands CodeAct is a single agent that is better at maintaining consistency in a long-horizon task, while OWL RolePlay adopts multi-agent collaboration and experiences difficulty in preserving progress and context.
Although the main agent then starts another round of delegation with a revised plan, the browsing agent often fails to pick up its previous progress due to UI complexity.

kp.k: Cost efficiency varies independently of headline capability
kp.d: Table 1 reports Gemini 2.5 Pro averaging 27.2 LLM calls and $4.2 per instance, compared with Gemini 2.0 Flash at 39.9 calls and $0.6, with 11.4% success. Costs measure model API token charges assuming no prompt caching, rather than a complete workplace deployment cost. Llama 3.1 405B achieves 7.4% success at $3.2 per instance; Llama 3.3 70B achieves 6.9% at $0.9. The authors treat smaller models’ similar performance as a promising efficiency trend.
qs: The number of steps is defined as the total number of LLM calls made during the task execution.
This suggests that open-weight models are not always the most cost-effective choice in agents given the serving cost, especially with highly complex tasks.
This suggests a promising future for LLM development, as smaller and more efficient models begin to catch up in agent performance.

kp.k: Simulated colleagues and judges introduce evaluation qualifications
kp.d: Claude-3-5-Sonnet-20241022 powers simulated colleagues and LLM evaluators across experiments. Appendix E reports that 51 tasks, or 29%, involve LLM evaluation, generally as a fallback after deterministic keyword matching. Appendix F reports that inspection of an early version of all 41 tasks involving simulated colleagues found one problematic trajectory arising from role-play prompt ambiguity, subsequently fixed. These are the authors’ reported checks, not proof that simulation and judging errors are impossible.
qs: In TheAgentCompany, there are 51 tasks (29%) involving LLM evaluation.
Furthermore, we first use deterministic keyword matches and then use LLM as a fallback.
Our use of LLM evaluation is a supplement to the deterministic evaluator, rather than a replacement.

A careful examination of the early version of all 41 tasks that simulated colleagues involved revealed only one trajectory with an issue that stemmed from role-play prompt ambiguity, which was already fixed in the latest TheAgentCompany version.

kp.k: Limited realism and absent human baselines constrain conclusions
kp.d: The authors acknowledge that automatically assessable tasks skew toward straightforward work, excluding complex creative activities such as product brainstorming and architecture design. Only two agent scaffolds are tested, task creation relies substantially on informed introspection, and no comparative human performance data were collected. Humans tested task feasibility, but this does not supply measured human speed or success rates. Proposed extensions include other industries, physical tasks, vaguer goals and longer end-to-end workflows.
qs: First, our tasks are generally on the more straightforward side due to the need to automatically evaluate with programs and test cases, and we do not cover more complex creative tasks such as brainstorming new product ideas or designing system architectures.
Second, we are only using two agent scaffolds as the baseline performance, and others may differ in performance.
During the construction of this benchmark, we had people test and complete all tasks to ensure the feasibility of the tasks and the evaluator. However, we did not collect human performance data.
Benchmarking may also be expanded with tasks that have more vague intents to better simulate real-world scenarios where the goal is not immediately clear at the very beginning.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Xu and coauthors claim that agents can autonomously complete a meaningful minority of simulated software-company tasks, but remain far from comprehensive workplace automation.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about digital work, not legal services. In the supplied September 2025 revision, the authors report that Gemini 2.5 Pro with OpenHands completes 30.3% of 175 tasks and earns 39.3% on a metric incorporating partial completion. They interpret this as evidence of selective task automation alongside substantial limitations on difficult, long-horizon work. These percentages describe benchmark tasks, not jobs eliminated or the share of actual employee work automated.

pts.k: The authors claim that automation difficulty does not track human perceptions of task difficulty: office workflows and social coordination can be harder for agents than software engineering.
pts.d: They identify communication, document understanding, complex interfaces and lengthy workflows as obstacles. Table 5 reports Gemini 2.5 Pro success rates of 37.68% for software engineering, 39.29% for project management and 34.48% for HR, versus 14.29% for data science, 13.33% for administration and 8.33% for finance. The proposed explanation that coding-focused development and public training data favor software engineering is explicitly a hypothesis, rather than a demonstrated causal result.

pts.k: The authors predict continuing capability and efficiency improvements, while arguing that open weights and multi-agent collaboration do not automatically deliver better workplace automation.
pts.d: Their forward-looking efficiency claim draws on comparisons among tested model generations: Llama 3.3 70B performs near Llama 3.1 405B at lower API cost, and Gemini 2.0 Flash provides comparatively inexpensive performance. They also report OpenHands at 8.6% success with GPT-4o versus 4.0% for OWL RolePlay configured with GPT-4o and o3-mini, attributing the latter's difficulties to preserving progress and context during delegation. These are findings about the tested configurations, not a universal ranking of single-agent and multi-agent systems.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a self-hosted, 175-task benchmark with executable checkpoints, supplemented by model comparisons and qualitative failure analysis.
pts.d: Tasks simulate a software startup using GitLab, ownCloud, Plane and RocketChat. Selection draws on O*NET 29.1, occupational employment and salary information, contributors' professional experience, and LLM-assisted brainstorming. Twenty contributors spent approximately 3,000 person-hours creating the benchmark. Completion is assessed principally through deterministic evaluators; 51 tasks (29%) involve LLM evaluation, and colleagues and LLM judges use a fixed Claude 3.5 Sonnet backbone. Full completion requires passing every checkpoint; the partial metric combines half the checkpoint fraction with half the full-completion indicator. Qualitative examples include failing to follow up with a colleague, getting stuck at a popup and renaming an unrelated user instead of contacting the intended person. API costs assume no prompt caching: the leading configuration averages 27.2 calls and $4.2 per evaluated instance, not a measured all-in cost per successfully completed human job. No systematic human performance comparison or actual enterprise productivity or displacement study is supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern the systems tested in the September 10, 2025 revision; future progress is anticipated without a dated forecast for job automation.
pts.d: The authors condition their conclusions on a simplified, non-embodied software-company environment and two agent scaffolds, with OpenHands versions differing across model configurations. Tasks have relatively clear goals and evaluable outputs; the benchmark excludes much complex creative work and does not comprehensively represent any occupation. The authors explicitly caution against inferring full-job automation from the results. The introduction's suggestion that most labor might be automatable within a couple of years is attributed to other sources, not adopted as the authors' own forecast. Predictions of increasing efficiency have no specified deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate subjects are software-company workers and employers; broader labor-market consequences are presented as possibilities rather than measured outcomes.
pts.d: The benchmark covers software engineers, project managers, data scientists, administrative staff, HR staff and finance staff. Employers considering adoption face uneven autonomous completion, workflow failures and differing model costs. The paper offers evidence about autonomous task execution, while suggesting that tasks within jobs may also be accelerated; it does not measure human-in-the-loop productivity gains. Economic policymakers and labor researchers are intended users of the findings. The authors mention improved quality of life and scientific progress alongside potential displacement and inequality, but provide no quantified causal estimates of these effects. They make no specific claims about lawyers, law firms, legal clients or legal markets.
